harbor.practice: Harbor uses retrieval for changing policy facts, a small SFT for the mandated answer format, and has not done continued pretraining because evaluation never showed a domain-language gap.
harbor.failure: Using fine-tuning as a substitute for a permission-aware database of changing facts.
harbor.fitNote: retrieval for facts, a small SFT for format
harbor.tryIt: Step through the pipeline figure and mark which stage each Harbor choice touches: retrieval for policy facts (no training), a small SFT for the answer format, and why continued pretraining was skipped.

store.fitNote: prices and stock change daily, so they stay out of the weights
store.practice: {company} considered continued pretraining on millions of listings to teach Indian product vocabulary. Evaluation showed the instruct model already handled most of it; a small SFT for {assistant}'s reply format plus retrieval over listings covered the rest at a fraction of the cost.
store.failure: Fine-tuning prices or stock levels into the model. They change daily, so they belong in retrieval and tools.
store.tryIt: Ask a base and an instruct model of the same size (for example SmolLM2-135M and SmolLM2-135M-Instruct, on CPU) to “Write a product description for a cotton kurta” and compare what each does.

bank.fitNote: format and refusals are tuning jobs; account facts are not
bank.practice: {company}'s assistant must follow a strict reply format and refuse to give investment advice. That is SFT and preference tuning on top of an instruct model; account facts come from systems of record at question time.
bank.failure: Fine-tuning on past customer conversations without removing personal data. The model can memorise and repeat it.
bank.tryIt: Write ten (instruction, ideal reply) pairs for dispute updates based on cases in disputes.csv, then five (chosen, rejected) pairs where the rejected reply promises a refund before the investigation ends.

travel.fitNote: booking formats are tuned; fares stay in tools
travel.practice: {company} keeps fares and rules in tools and retrieval, and uses SFT only to teach {assistant} its booking-confirmation format and when to ask a clarifying question.
travel.failure: Training the model on last year's fare rules. It will state outdated change fees with confidence.
travel.tryIt: Compare a base and an instruct small model on “Confirm the booking change: Goa hotel moved by two days” and note which one follows the instruction.

harbor.practice: For any Harbor fine-tune, the dataset manifest records source, licence decision, content hash, language and filter outcome, and evaluation document families are excluded before training sequences are built.
harbor.failure: Assuming publicly reachable text is licensed for any training or redistribution purpose.
harbor.fitNote: policy revisions are near-duplicates by design
harbor.tryIt: Run MinHash near-duplicate detection (for example with the datasketch library) on policies.json and check that each policy is grouped with its older revisions.

store.fitNote: sellers copy descriptions across many listings
store.practice: {company} fine-tuned on seller descriptions and reviews. Many sellers copy the same description across hundreds of listings, so near-duplicate removal shrank the set by about a third and stopped the model memorising one seller's wording.
store.failure: Training on scraped competitor listings or reviews without checking their terms of use and licences.
store.tryIt: Shingle the titles in products.csv into word 3-grams, compute the Jaccard similarity of every pair, and list the near-duplicates above 0.6.

bank.fitNote: PII scrubbing and evaluation-overlap checks before any fine-tune
bank.practice: {company}'s training data for the dispute assistant passes PII scrubbing (account numbers, names, phone numbers) and a licence and consent check before any fine-tune, and evaluation cases are removed from training by n-gram overlap.
bank.failure: Assuming internal data is free to train on. Customer consent and data-protection rules still apply.
bank.tryIt: Write a regex scrubber for account-like numbers and phone numbers, run it on the texts in disputes.csv and count what it catches. Then check 13-gram overlap between a training split and an evaluation split.

travel.practice: {company} trains little of its own. Its corpus work is mostly deduplicating fare-rule documents from several suppliers before indexing them (10.4).
travel.failure: Indexing the same rule from three suppliers as three sources. Answers cite whichever comes first, even if it is outdated.
travel.tryIt: Copy two rules in fare_rules.json with small wording changes and check that MinHash similarity flags them.

harbor.practice: Harbor's team used C = 6ND to show that pretraining even a 1B model on their 20B-token corpus would cost far more than adapting an existing open model, which ended the discussion.
harbor.failure: Repeating a small corpus to reach a big token count and expecting the diversity of a larger corpus.
harbor.tryIt: In the calculator, enter 1B parameters at 20 tokens per parameter (Harbor's 20B-token corpus) and read the GPU-hours. Then explain why the team still preferred adapting an existing open model: quality, not only cost.

store.fitNote: pricing a home-grown model before building it
store.practice: {company} asked whether to pretrain its own 3B model. C = 6ND at about 1,000 tokens per parameter gives roughly 37,000 GPU-hours for the final run alone, before any experiments, against a few GPU-hours to adapt an open model with LoRA.
store.failure: Budgeting compute for the final run only. Experiments, failed runs and evaluation add substantially to it.
store.tryIt: In the calculator, enter 3B parameters, 1,000 tokens per parameter, 40% MFU and 64 GPUs and read the days. Then halve the MFU and see what happens.

bank.practice: {company} will not pretrain. Scaling relationships matter to it only when choosing which size of model to self-host: a smaller model trained for longer is cheaper to serve for millions of case summaries.
bank.failure: Choosing the largest model on a benchmark without pricing its serving cost per case.
bank.tryIt: Use the calculator to compare an 8B model at 2,000 tokens per parameter with a 70B model at 20, and note which is cheaper to train and which is cheaper to serve.

travel.fitNote: a language mix for a small intent model
travel.practice: {company}'s mixture question is small but real: how much Hindi, Tamil and Hinglish to include when training its intent model, so that no language is under-served.
travel.failure: Training the intent model on the natural traffic mix only, so Tamil (about 7% of bookings) gets too few examples to learn from.
travel.tryIt: Count bookings by language in bookings.csv and choose a training mix for an intent classifier. Then describe how you would test whether the Tamil share is enough.

harbor.practice: Before each Harbor SFT run, an engineer renders one example with the model's chat template and checks that only the assistant tokens carry labels.
harbor.failure: Launching a run with a mismatched chat template or wrong loss mask; training will run and still optimise the wrong tokens.
harbor.fitNote: rendering the template and checking labels before SFT
harbor.tryIt: Render one Harbor-style conversation with a model's tokenizer.apply_chat_template and print which tokens would get label −100. Compare with the figure.

store.fitNote: tool calls and results inside shopping conversations
store.practice: {company}'s SFT set for {assistant} has a system prompt, a shopper turn, a tool call to the order API, the tool result and the reply. The assistant turns, including the tool-call text, carry labels; the tool result is masked.
store.failure: Training on synthetic conversations generated by a model whose licence forbids using its output to train other models.
store.tryIt: Write one SFT record in JSON for the Hinglish chat “Refund kab milega? UPI se pay kiya tha.” from chats.json, with a tool call and its result, then mark which tokens should be masked.

bank.fitNote: refusals as training examples, rendered with the right template
bank.practice: {company}'s SFT records include refusals: the assistant declines to give investment advice and points to the right channel. Every record is rendered with the target model's chat template before training.
bank.failure: Fine-tuning with one model family's template and serving with another's. Quality drops silently.
bank.tryIt: Render the same dispute conversation with two different models' chat templates and diff the token sequences.

travel.fitNote: multi-step tool calls are the training data
travel.practice: {assistant}'s training conversations are multi-step: search flights, hold a seat, confirm, with tool calls and results in between. The loss covers the assistant's tool-call arguments, which is where most errors happen.
travel.failure: Masking the tool-call turns along with the tool results. The model then never learns to write correct arguments.
travel.tryIt: Turn one request from messages.json into a multi-turn record with two tool calls, and label each span as trained or masked.

harbor.practice: Harbor's extraction reward checks schema validity and exact field values, so an empty but valid JSON object scores zero instead of full marks.
harbor.failure: Treating reward score, human preference, correctness and policy compliance as the same measurement.
harbor.fitNote: a reward that cannot be satisfied by empty output
harbor.tryIt: Write a reward function for Harbor's extraction task that scores an empty but valid JSON object as zero, then try to game it with three outputs a model might learn to produce.

store.practice: {company} builds DPO pairs from support cases: the chosen reply follows the returns policy and offers an exchange; the rejected one promises an immediate refund the policy does not allow.
store.failure: Rewarding shopper thumbs-up alone. The model learns to promise refunds and discounts that make shoppers happy and cost money.
store.tryIt: Write ten DPO pairs from situations you can find in orders.csv (a late delivery, a return outside the window) and check each chosen reply against the returns rule.

bank.fitNote: policy-compliant refusals make clear preference pairs
bank.practice: {company}'s preference data teaches caution: the chosen reply explains the dispute process and timeline; the rejected one confirms a refund before investigation or gives investment advice.
bank.failure: Rewarding length or politeness without checking policy compliance. A reward model can favour long, apologetic replies that still break the rules.
bank.tryIt: Write five (chosen, rejected) pairs for cases in disputes.csv, then write a verifier that rejects any reply promising a refund before the case outcome is known.

travel.fitNote: verifiable rewards for complete, correct bookings
travel.practice: {company} trains its booking agent with verifiable rewards in a sandbox: an episode scores 1 only if the final booking matches the request (dates, travellers, fare rule) and nothing extra was booked.
travel.failure: A reward that only checks that a booking exists. The agent learns to book anything, quickly.
travel.tryIt: Write a verifier for “cheapest flight Bengaluru to Delhi next Friday morning, 2 adults” that checks a booked option against a small inventory you define, including one trap option that is cheaper but in the evening.

harbor.practice: Harbor's one larger fine-tune ran on 8 GPUs with FSDP; the team measured 5.6× speed-up, not 8×, because of communication overhead.
harbor.failure: Expecting N GPUs to give N times the throughput.
harbor.fitNote: an 8-GPU FSDP run that scaled 5.6×, not 8×
harbor.tryIt: In the ZeRO calculator, set 8B parameters on 8 GPUs of 80 GB and step through stages 1 to 3. Then explain why Harbor's run scaled 5.6×, not 8×.

store.practice: {company} does not train large language models. Its largest job, an image-tagging fine-tune, fits on one node with plain data parallelism.
store.failure: Adding nodes to a small job and getting slower runs because communication dominates.
store.tryIt: In the pipeline figure, set 4 stages and 2, 8 and 32 micro-batches, and read the idle fraction each time.

bank.fitNote: a full fine-tune that does not fit, so QLoRA
bank.practice: {company} wanted to fully fine-tune a 70B model for case summaries on its own 8 × 80 GB node. The sharding numbers showed about 1.1 TB of training state, so it fine-tuned with QLoRA instead (13.3).
bank.failure: Requesting GPUs from a parameter count without applying the 16-bytes-per-parameter rule.
bank.tryIt: In the ZeRO calculator, enter 70B on 8 GPUs of 80 GB and confirm it does not fit even at stage 3. Then find the GPU count at which stage 3 fits, before activations.

travel.practice: {company} runs no multi-GPU training. The topic matters to it only when reading vendors' claims about how their hosted models were trained.
travel.failure: Treating a vendor's training-cluster size as evidence of quality on your own tasks.
travel.tryIt: Step through the data-parallel figure and write one sentence on why all four copies stay identical after the update.

harbor.practice: New Harbor engineers train the browser bigram model and the NumPy lab (Appendix A) in their first week, so later discussions about loss, validation and checkpoints share one picture.
harbor.failure: Reading plausible samples from a tiny memorised corpus as evidence of generalisation.
harbor.fitNote: a shared picture of loss, validation and checkpoints
harbor.tryIt: Replace the bigram figure's corpus with a few paragraphs from policies.json, train 200 steps and sample. Compare the loss with the dashed uniform-guess line.

store.practice: {company}'s new data scientists train the bigram model on product titles. It quickly learns brand names and sizes, a vivid demonstration of memorisation on a small, repetitive corpus.
store.failure: Reading fluent-looking titles from a tiny model as evidence that it understands products.
store.tryIt: Paste 30 titles from products.csv into the bigram figure's corpus, train, sample at temperatures 0.5 and 1.5, and note how often a sample is an exact copy of a training title.

bank.fitNote: a full lifecycle model-risk reviewers can follow
bank.practice: {company} uses the Appendix A lab to show model-risk reviewers a full lifecycle on a toy problem: splits, a baseline, checkpoint selection and a reload check.
bank.failure: Treating a toy model's validation result as evidence about production.
bank.tryIt: Run the Appendix A script on the policy texts in policies.json and report its test loss against the unigram baseline.

travel.fitNote: different scripts change the vocabulary and the baseline
travel.practice: {company} trains the bigram model on Hindi and Tamil messages to show how a character-level model handles other scripts: the vocabulary grows, so the uniform-guess line rises.
travel.failure: Comparing losses across corpora with different vocabularies. The uniform baseline differs.
travel.tryIt: Paste the Hindi messages from messages.json into the bigram corpus box and train, then compare the dashed ln(vocabulary) line with the English corpus.

harbor.scenario: Use the text of policies.json as the corpus. In the manifest, record the source as “synthetic, generated by scripts/make_datasets.py”, the licence as the repository's MIT licence, and exclude outdated revisions (current: false) from the test split so the test text is not a near-copy of training text.

store.scenario: Build the corpus from titles in products.csv and the English reviews in reviews.json. Note how quickly the model memorises repeated brand names, and record in the manifest that titles are templated, so held-out loss overstates generalisation.

bank.scenario: Use the policy texts in policies.json plus the English dispute texts in disputes.csv. Run a PII scrub before building the corpus and record its result in the manifest, as {company} would for real data.

travel.scenario: Use fare_rules.json plus the messages in messages.json. Train once on English only and once with Hindi and Tamil included, and compare the vocabulary size and the uniform-guess loss.
